## 🎯 The task

Today you are issued **your own time series**, and it stays yours for the rest of the course.

This lab asks you to take it apart and forecast it from its parts: decompose it, forecast the
seasonally adjusted series, carry the seasonal component forward, put them back together — and then
compare the result honestly against the four simple methods from Week 1. Toolbox only: no ETS, no
ARIMA. Those are Weeks 6 and 7, on this same series.

::: {.callout-important}
## This one counts

8 points. **Deadline: 23:59 today**, on Moodle. Marks and comments come back before the next
practice session.
:::

## 🗂 Your series

Your series is issued by a hash of the **same identifier you have used since Week 1**. The template
does it for you: it turns your identifier into a code such as `TS-4DD7A` and downloads that series.

::: {.callout-note}
## What "anonymised" means here

The series is real. What has been removed is its identity: no name, no units, values rescaled,
the calendar shifted by whole years, the history trimmed. Two students never get the same window of
the same series, so a forecast is worth exactly what your model is worth.

You are not expected to work out what it measures, and you will not be marked for trying. Read the
data, not the domain.
:::

**This series is yours for Weeks 6, 7, 8 and 9 as well.** Every series in the pool is seasonal, has
at least fifteen years of history, and has been checked so that both an automatic ETS and an
automatic ARIMA beat its benchmark — which is what makes the challenges from Week 6 a fair fight.

## Why accuracy is not marked this week — and is from Week 6

The plan was to mark this week on whether you beat your benchmark. Before setting that, the odds
were measured on the actual pool, and they do not support it:

| Benchmark | Decomposition forecast beats it |
|---|---:|
| the best of the four simple methods, chosen on a validation window | **36%** |
| a plain `naive` forecast | **96%** |

A target you clear 36% of the time no matter how well you work is luck, and one you clear 96% of the
time is a formality. Neither is worth three points. So this week the points go to the work itself —
how the decomposition is done, and how well you argue from it — and **accuracy is measured but not
marked**: your score against all four simple methods is published the next morning as information.

From Week 6 that changes. With ETS, and then with ARIMA, every series in the pool is one where the
method of that week does beat the benchmark — so the accuracy points start when they measure your
model rather than your draw. This week's number is the baseline they will be compared against.
:::

## 📊 Section 1 — EDA and visualisation (1 point)

This is a series you have never seen. The plots are here to justify the decisions in Section 2, not
to fill space.

- A time plot, always.
- Whichever of the seasonal, subseries and ACF plots your argument actually uses.
- The validation split on a plot: history, validation window, and your forecast over it.
- One sentence per plot. **A plot with no reading attached earns nothing.**

## 📐 Section 2 — Decomposition and forecast (3 points)

| Item | Points | What earns them |
|---|---:|---|
| 2.1 | 1 | **The decomposition.** STL with `period` equal to your series' seasonal period, components plotted, and the seasonally adjusted series computed from it. A decomposition with the wrong period earns nothing here, and nothing after it. |
| 2.2 | 1 | **The forecast, built from the parts.** The seasonally adjusted series forecast with a simple method, the seasonal component carried forward, the two added back. Candidates compared on the **validation window** — the last $h$ observations — with MASE, against all four simple methods. |
| 2.3 | 1 | **The submission.** Your chosen approach refit on the **whole** history, $h$ steps ahead, with an 80% interval, written to the submission file by the notebook. |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Where this goes wrong

- The seasonal period is `M` from the setup cell — 12 for monthly series, 4 for quarterly. Not the number of
  years, not 7.
- Forecast the **adjusted** series, not the raw one, and add the season back afterwards. Doing one
  without the other is the most common way to lose both marks in 2.2.
- `STL` needs `seasonal` to be an odd integer ≥ 3, and an `int`.
- Refit on the whole history before forecasting the hidden horizon. Forecasting from the training
  part only throws away your last $h$ observations — the most informative ones you have.

📖 [FPP 5.7 forecasting with decomposition](https://otexts.com/fpp3/forecasting-decomposition.html) ·
[FPP 5.4 residual diagnostics](https://otexts.com/fpp3/diagnostics.html) ·
[FPP 5.8 evaluating accuracy](https://otexts.com/fpp3/accuracy.html) ·
[FPP the Pythonic Way, ch. 5](https://otexts.com/fpppy/nbs/05-toolbox.html)
:::

### Your benchmark, for comparison

The template computes it: the **best of the four simple methods** — `mean`, `naive`, `snaive`,
`drift` — chosen by RMSE on the validation window, then refit on the whole history. It is not a
target you are marked against this week, but it is the number Section 3 argues with, and the one the
published score will use.

## ✍️ Section 3 — Justification block (3 points)

Three points, and the part a human reads closely. Roughly a paragraph each, with numbers from your
own cells rather than adjectives.

| Item | Points | What earns them |
|---|---:|---|
| 3.1 | 0.75 | **What the data shows.** Frequency, seasonal period, trend, level shifts, outliers — each claim tied to a plot from Section 1. |
| 3.2 | 0.75 | **Why this decomposition and this level method.** Your choice of `seasonal` and `robust`, and of the method that forecasts the adjusted series, tied to what you just described. Say what you tried and dropped. |
| 3.3 | 0.75 | **What the residuals say.** ACF and a Ljung-Box test on your final model's residuals, read: what structure is left, and what it damages — the point forecast or the interval. |
| 3.4 | 0.75 | **What you expect.** Your MASE on the validation window against all four simple methods, and what you expect on the hidden horizon. If you expect to lose to a simple method, say which and why. |

::: {.callout-important}
Marked on the reasoning. A decomposition forecast that loses to seasonal naive and explains exactly
why scores full marks here; one that wins and cannot say why does not.
:::

## 🧹 Section 4 — Code quality and reproducibility (1 point)

- The notebook runs top to bottom on a fresh kernel without errors.
- The submission file is written **by the notebook**, not edited by hand.
- No leakage: nothing after the end of your history exists, so nothing can be fitted to it. If you
  tuned on the validation window, say so in 3.2 — that is legitimate, and it is also why your
  validation MASE is optimistic.
- Every number in your text comes from a cell.
